s: 2 Corinthians 1:14.—As you also have acknowledged us in part, that we are your rejoicing, even as you also are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus.
The apostle, in the earlier part of the chapter, declares what great troubles he met with in the course of his ministry.
In the text and the two verses before it, he declares what his comforts and supports were under the troubles he met with.
There are four things in particular.

1. That he had approved himself to his own conscience, verse 12: “For this is our rejoicing, the testimony of our conscience: that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not by fleshly wisdom but by the grace of God, we have conducted ourselves in the world, and all the more so toward you.”

2. Another thing he speaks of as a matter of comfort is that, as he had approved himself to his own conscience, so he had also to the consciences of his hearers, the Corinthians, to whom he was now writing, and that they would approve of him at the day of judgment.
3. The hope he had of seeing the blessed fruit of his labors and sufferings in the ministry, in their happiness and glory, in that great day of accounts.
4. That, in his ministry among the Corinthians, he had approved himself to his Judge, who would approve and reward his faithfulness in that day.

These last three particulars are signified in my text and the preceding verse; and, indeed, all four are implied in the text. It is implied that the Corinthians had acknowledged him as their spiritual father and as one who had been faithful among them, and as the means of their future joy and glory at the day of judgment, and as one whom they would then see, and have a joyful meeting with as such. It is implied that the apostle expected at that time to have a joyful meeting with them before the Judge, and with joy to behold their glory, as the fruit of his labors; and so they would be his rejoicing. It is implied also that he then expected to be approved by the great Judge, when he and they should meet together before him; and that the Judge would then acknowledge his faithfulness, and that this had been the means of their glory; and that thus he would, as it were, give them to him as his crown of rejoicing.
But the apostle could not hope for this unless he had the testimony of his own conscience in his favor.
And therefore the words imply, in the strongest manner, that he had approved himself to his own conscience.
There is one thing implied in each of these particulars, and in every part of the text, which is the point I shall make the subject of my present discourse, namely:
Ministers, and the people who are under their care, must meet one another before Christ’s tribunal at the day of judgment.

Ministers, and the people who have been under their care, must be parted in this world, however well they have been united: if they are not separated before, they must be parted by death; and they may be separated while life continues.

We live in a world of change, where nothing is certain or stable; and where a little time, a few revolutions of the sun, bring to pass strange things, surprising alterations, in particular persons, in families, in towns and churches, in countries and nations.
It often happens that those who seem most united are, in a little time, most disunited, and at the greatest distance.

Thus ministers and people, between whom there has been the greatest mutual regard and the closest union, may not only differ in their judgments and be estranged in affection, but one may tear away from the other, and all relation between them be dissolved; the minister may be removed to a distant place, and they may never have anything more to do with one another in this world.
But if it is so, there is one more meeting that they must have, and that is on the last great day of accounts.
Here I would show,
I. In what manner ministers, and the people who have been under their care, shall meet one another at the day of judgment.
II. For what purposes.
III. For what reasons God has so ordered it that ministers and their people shall then meet together in such a manner, and for such purposes.
I. I would show, in some particulars, in what manner ministers, and the people who have been under their care, shall meet one another at the day of judgment.
Concerning this I would observe two things in general.
1. That they shall not then meet only as all mankind must then meet, but there will be something distinctive in the manner of their meeting.
2. That their meeting together at that time shall be very different from what used to take place in the house of God in this world.
1. They shall not meet on that day as all the world must then meet together.
I would observe a difference in two things.
(1) As to a clear, actual view, and a distinct knowledge and notice of each other.

Although the whole world will then be present, all mankind of all generations gathered in one vast assembly, with all of the angelic nature, both elect and fallen angels; yet we need not suppose that everyone will have a distinct and particular knowledge of each individual of the whole assembled multitude, which will undoubtedly consist of many millions of millions.

Though it is probable that men’s capacities will be much greater than in the present state, yet they will not be infinite; though their understanding and comprehension will be vastly extended, yet men will not be made gods.

Particular persons will probably have a very enlarged view of various parts and members of that vast assembly, and so of the proceedings of that great day; but yet it must be that, according to the nature of finite minds, some persons and some things on that day shall fall more under the notice of particular persons than others; and this (as we may well suppose) according as they shall have a nearer concern with some than with others in the transactions of the day.

There will be special reason why those who have had special concerns together in this world, in their state of probation, and whose mutual affairs will then be tried and judged, should especially be set in one another’s view.

Thus we may suppose that rulers and subjects, earthly judges and those whom they have judged, neighbors who have had mutual interaction, dealings and disputes, heads of families and their children and servants, shall then meet, and be set together in a special way.

And this will especially be so with ministers and their people. It is evident from the text that these shall be in each other’s view, shall distinctly know each other, and shall take particular notice of one another at that time.
(2) They shall meet together as having a special concern with one another in the great transactions of that day.
Although they shall meet the whole world at that time, yet they will not have any immediate and particular concern with all.
Indeed, the far greater part of those who shall then be gathered together will be such as they have had no dealings with in their state of probation, and so will have no mutual concerns to be judged.

But as to ministers, and the people who have been under their care, they will be such as have had much immediate concern with one another, in matters of the greatest importance that mankind ever have to do with one another in.
Therefore they especially must meet and be brought together before the Judge, as having special concern with one another in the design and business of that great day of accounts.
Thus their meeting, as to its manner, will be different from the meeting of mankind in general.
2. Their meeting at the day of judgment will be very different from their meetings with one another in this world.
Ministers and their people, while their relation continues, often meet together in this world.
They are accustomed to meet from Sabbath to Sabbath, and at other times, for the public worship of God, and the administration of ordinances, and the solemn services of God’s house.

And besides these meetings, they also have occasions to meet for deciding and managing their church affairs, for the exercise of church discipline, and for settling and adjusting those things which concern the purity and good order of public administrations.
But their meeting at the day of judgment will be exceedingly different, in its manner and circumstances, from any such meetings and interviews as they have with one another in the present state.
I would observe how, in a few particulars.
(1) Now they meet together in a preparatory, changeable state, but then in an unchangeable state.

Now sinners in the congregation meet their minister in a state in which they are capable of a saving change, capable of being turned, through God’s blessing on the ministrations and labors of their pastor, from the power of Satan to God; and of being brought out of a state of guilt, condemnation and wrath, into a state of peace and favor with God, to the enjoyment of the privileges of his children, and a title to their eternal inheritance.

And saints now meet their minister with great remains of corruption, and sometimes under great spiritual difficulties and affliction; and therefore they are still proper subjects for the means of a happy alteration of their state, consisting in a greater freedom from these things, which they have reason to hope for by way of attending on the ordinances, and of which God is commonly pleased to make his ministers the instruments.
And ministers and their people now meet in order to bring about such happy changes; these are the great benefits sought in their solemn meetings in this world.
But when they meet together at the day of judgment, it will be far otherwise.
They will not then meet in order to use means for bringing about any such changes; for they will all meet in an unchangeable state.

Sinners will be in an unchangeable state: those who shall then be under the guilt and power of sin, and have the wrath of God abiding on them, shall be beyond all remedy or possibility of change, and shall meet their ministers without any hope of relief or remedy, or of getting any good by their means.

And as for the saints, they will already be perfectly delivered from all their formerly remaining corruption, temptation, and calamities of every kind, and set forever out of their reach; and no deliverance, no happy alteration, will remain to be accomplished by the use of the means of grace under the administrations of ministers.
It will then be pronounced, “Let him who is unjust be unjust still; and let him who is filthy be filthy still; and let him who is righteous be righteous still; and let him who is holy be holy still.”
(2) Then they shall meet together in a state of clear, certain and infallible light.

Ministers are set as guides and teachers, and are represented in Scripture as lights set up in the churches; and in the present state they meet their people from time to time in order to instruct and enlighten them, to correct their mistakes, and to be a voice behind them when they turn aside to the right hand or to the left, saying, “This is the way; walk in it”; to demonstrate and confirm the truth by setting forth the proper evidences of it, and to refute errors and corrupt opinions, to convince those in error and establish those who doubt.

But when Christ comes to judgment, every error and false opinion shall be detected; all deceit and illusion shall vanish away before the light of that day, as the darkness of the night vanishes at the appearance of the rising sun; and every doctrine of the word of God shall then appear in full evidence, and none shall remain unconvinced; all shall know the truth with the greatest certainty, and there shall be no mistakes to correct.

Now ministers and their people may disagree in their judgments concerning some matters of religion, and may sometimes meet to confer together about those things in which they differ, and to hear the reasons that may be offered on one side and the other; and all may be ineffective as to any conviction of the truth: they may meet and part again, no more agreed than before; and the side which was in the wrong may remain so still. Sometimes the meetings of ministers with their people, in such a case of disagreeing opinions, are accompanied by unhappy debate and controversy, conducted with much prejudice and lack of candor; not tending to light and conviction, but rather to confirm and increase darkness, and to establish opposition to the truth and the estrangement of affection from one another.

But when they shall hereafter meet together at the day of judgment, before the tribunal of the great Judge, the mind and will of Christ will be made known; and there shall no longer be any debate or difference of opinion; the evidence of the truth shall appear beyond all dispute, and all controversies shall be finally and forever decided.

Now ministers meet their people in order to enlighten and awaken the consciences of sinners: setting before them the great evil and danger of sin, the strictness of God’s law, their own wickedness of heart and practice, the great guilt they are under, the wrath that abides upon them, and their powerlessness, blindness, poverty, and helpless and ruined condition: but all is often in vain; notwithstanding all their ministers can say, they still remain dull and unawakened, and their consciences unconvinced.

But it will not be so at their last meeting at the day of judgment. Sinners, when they meet their minister before their great Judge, will not meet him with a dull conscience: they will then be fully convinced of the truth of those things which they formerly heard from him, concerning the greatness and terrible majesty of God, his holiness and hatred of sin, and his awful justice in punishing it, the strictness of his law, and the dreadfulness and truth of his threatenings, and their own unspeakable guilt and misery; and they shall never again be insensible of these things: the eyes of conscience will then be fully enlightened, and shall never be blinded again; the mouth of conscience shall then be opened, and shall never be shut any more.

Now ministers meet with their people, in public and private, in order to enlighten them concerning the state of their souls; to open and apply the rules of God’s word to them, so that they may search their own hearts and discern the state they are in.
But now ministers have no infallible discernment of the state of the souls of their own people; and the most skillful of them are liable to mistakes, and often are mistaken in things of this nature.

Nor are the people able to know with certainty the state of their minister, or one another’s state; very often those who pass among them for saints, and perhaps eminent saints, are great hypocrites; and on the other hand, those are sometimes censured, or hardly received into their charity, who are indeed some of God’s jewels.

And nothing is more common than for men to be mistaken concerning their own state: many who are abominable to God, and the children of his wrath, think highly of themselves as his precious saints and dear children.

Indeed, there is reason to think that often some who are most bold in their confidence of their safe and happy state, and think themselves not only true saints but the most eminent saints in the congregation, are in a peculiar manner a smoke in God’s nose.

And so it undoubtedly often is in those congregations where the word of God is most faithfully dispensed, notwithstanding all that ministers can say in their clearest explanations and most searching applications of the doctrines and rules of God’s word to the souls of their hearers, in their meetings with one another.
But on the day of judgment they shall have another sort of meeting; then the secrets of every heart shall be made manifest, and every man’s state shall be perfectly known, as in 1 Corinthians 4,

verse 5: “Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make known the purposes of the hearts; and then every man shall have praise from God.”
Then none shall be deceived concerning his own state, nor be in doubt about it any longer.
There shall be an eternal end to all the false conceit and vain hopes of deluded hypocrites, and to all the doubts and fears of sincere Christians.

And then all shall know the state of one another’s souls: the people shall know whether their minister has been sincere and faithful, and the ministers shall know the state of every one of their people, and to whom the word and ordinances of God have been an aroma of life to life, and to whom an aroma of death to death.

Now in this present state it often happens that when ministers and people meet together to debate and manage their church affairs, especially in a state of controversy, they are ready to judge and censure one another with regard to each other’s views and designs, and the principles and ends by which each is influenced; and are greatly mistaken in their judgment, and wrong one another with regard to each other’s views and designs and the principles and ends by which each is influenced, and are greatly mistaken in their judgment, and wrong one another in their censures.

But at that future meeting, things will be set in a true and perfect light, and the principles and aims from which everyone has acted shall be certainly known; and there will be an end to all errors of this kind, and all unrighteous censures.
(3) In this world, ministers and their people often meet together to hear of and wait upon an unseen Lord; but at the day of judgment they shall meet in his most immediate and visible presence.

Ministers, who now often meet their people to preach to them the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, to convince them that there is a God, and to declare to them what manner of being he is, and to convince them that he governs and will judge the world, and that there is a future state of rewards and punishments, and to preach to them a Christ in heaven and at the right hand of God in an unseen world, shall then meet their people in the most immediate and perceptible presence of this great God, Savior and Judge, appearing in the most plain, visible and open manner, with great glory, with all his holy angels, before them and the whole world.

They shall not meet them to hear about an absent Christ, an unseen Lord and future Judge; but to appear before that Judge, and to be set together in the presence of that supreme Lord, in his immense glory and awesome majesty, of whom they have heard so often in their meetings together on earth.
(4) The meeting, on the last day, of ministers and the people who have been under their care, will not be attended by anyone with a careless, heedless heart.

With such a heart their meetings in this world are often attended by many persons, having little regard for him whom they profess to adore together in the solemn duties of his public worship, taking little heed to their own thoughts or the frame of their minds, not attending to the business they are engaged in, or considering the end for which they have come together.

But the meeting on that great day will be very different: there will not be one careless heart, no sleeping, no wandering of mind from the great concern of the meeting, no inattentiveness to the business of the day, no disregard of the presence they are in, or of those great things which they shall hear from Christ at that meeting, or which they formerly heard from him and of him by their ministers, in their meetings in a state of trial, or which they shall then hear their ministers declaring concerning them before their Judge.

Having observed these things concerning the manner and circumstances of this future meeting of ministers and the people who have been under their care, before the tribunal of Christ at the day of judgment, I now proceed,
II. To observe for what purposes they shall then meet.
1. To give an account, before the great Judge, of their behavior toward one another in the relation they stood in to each other in this world.

Ministers are sent forth by Christ to their people on his business; they are his servants and messengers; and, when they have finished their service, they must return to their master to give him an account of what they have done, and of the reception they have had in performing their ministry.
Thus we find, in Luke 14,

verses 16–21, that when the servant who was sent out to call the guests to the great supper had done his errand, and finished his appointed service, he returned to his master and gave him an account of what he had done, and of the reception he had received.
And when the master, being angry, sent his servant to others, he returns again and gives his master an account of his conduct and success.
So we read, in Hebrews 13,
verse 17, of ministers being rulers in the house of God, “who watch for souls, as those who must give account.”

And we see by the aforementioned Luke 14 that ministers must give an account to their master, not only of their own behavior in the discharge of their office, but also of their people’s reception of them, and of the treatment they have met with among them.

And therefore, as they will be called to give an account of both, they shall give an account at the great day of accounts in the presence of their people; they and their people both being present before their Judge.

Faithful ministers will then give an account with joy concerning those who have received them well and made good use of their ministry; and these will be given to them, on that day, as their crown of rejoicing.

And at the same time they will give an account of the ill treatment of those who have not received them and their messages from Christ well: they will meet these, not as they used to do in this world, to counsel and warn them, but to bear witness against them, and, as their judges and assessors with Christ, to condemn them.

And on the other hand, the people will, on that day, rise up in judgment against wicked and unfaithful ministers who have sought their own temporal interest more than the good of the souls of their flock.

2. At that time ministers, and the people who have been under their care, shall meet together before Christ, so that he may judge between them as to any controversies which have existed between them in this world.
So it very often happens in this evil world that great differences and controversies arise between ministers and the people who are under their pastoral care.

Though they are under the greatest obligations to live in peace, more than persons in almost any relation whatever; and although contests and dissensions between persons so related are, on many accounts, the most unhappy and terrible in their consequences of any sort of contention; yet how frequent such contentions have been!

Sometimes a people contend with their ministers about their doctrine, sometimes about their administrations and conduct, and sometimes about their financial support; and sometimes such contests continue a long time; and sometimes they are decided in this world according to the prevailing interest of one party or the other, rather than by the word of God and the reason of things; and sometimes such controversies never have any proper resolution in this world.
But at the day of judgment there will be a full, perfect and everlasting decision of them.

The infallible Judge, the infinite fountain of light, truth and justice, will judge between the contending parties, and will declare what the truth is, who is in the right, and what agrees with his mind and will.

And for this purpose the parties must stand together before him on the last day, which will be the great day of finishing and determining all controversies, correcting all mistakes, and abolishing all unrighteous judgments, errors and confusions, which have existed before in the world of mankind.

3. Ministers, and the people who have been under their care, must meet together at that time to receive an eternal sentence and retribution from the Judge, in the presence of each other, according to their behavior in the relation they stood in to one another in the present state.
The Judge will not only declare justice, but he will do justice between ministers and their people.

He will declare what is right between them, approving him who has been just and faithful, and condemning the unjust; and perfect truth and equity shall prevail in the sentence which he passes, in the rewards he bestows and the punishments which he inflicts.
There shall be a glorious reward to faithful ministers: to those who have been successful, Daniel 12,

verse 3: “And those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the heavens; and those who turn many to righteousness, as the stars forever and ever”; and also to those who have been faithful, and yet not successful, Isaiah 49,
verse 4: “Then I said, I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing; yet surely my judgment is with the Lord, and my reward with my God.”
And those who have received and welcomed them well shall be gloriously rewarded, Matthew 10,
verses 40, 41: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.
Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward.”
Such people and their faithful ministers shall be each other’s crown of rejoicing, 1 Thessalonians 2,
verses 19, 20: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing?
Are not you yourselves, in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming?
For you are our glory and joy.”
And in the text: We are your rejoicing, as you also are ours, in the day of the Lord Jesus.
But those who mistreat Christ’s faithful ministers, especially in that in which they are faithful, shall be severely punished, Matthew 10,
verses 14, 15: “And whoever does not receive you or hear your words, when you leave that house or city, shake the dust off your feet.
Truly I say to you, it shall be more bearable for the sinners of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city.”
Deuteronomy 33:8–11: “And of Levi he said, Let your Urim and your Thummim be with your holy one....
They shall teach Jacob your judgments, and Israel your law....
Bless, Lord, his substance, and accept the work of his hands; strike through the loins of those who rise against him, and of those who hate him, so that they rise no more.”
On the other hand, those ministers who are found to have been unfaithful shall have a most terrible punishment.
See Ezekiel 33:6; Matthew 23:1–33.
Thus justice shall be administered on the great day to ministers and their people.

And to that end they shall meet together, that they may not only receive justice themselves, but see justice done to the other party: for this is the purpose of that great day, to reveal or declare the righteous judgment of God, Romans 2,
verse 5. Ministers shall have justice done to them, and they shall see justice done to their people; and the people shall receive justice and see justice done to their minister.

And so all things will be adjusted and settled forever between them; everyone being sentenced and repaid according to his works, either in receiving and wearing a crown of eternal joy and glory, or in suffering everlasting shame and pain.
I come now to the next thing proposed, namely,

III. To give some reasons why we may suppose God has so ordered it that ministers, and the people who have been under their care, shall meet together at the day of judgment in such a manner and for such purposes.
There are two things which I would now observe:
1. The mutual concerns of ministers and their people are of the greatest importance.

The Scripture declares that God will bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it is good or whether it is evil. It is fitting that all the concerns and all the behavior of mankind, both public and private, should be brought at last before God’s tribunal and finally determined by an infallible Judge; but it is especially necessary that it should be so with affairs of very great importance.

Now the mutual concerns of a Christian minister and his church and congregation are of the vastest importance: in many respects, of much greater moment than the temporal concerns of the greatest earthly monarchs and their kingdoms or empires.

It is of vast consequence how ministers discharge their office and conduct themselves toward their people in the work of the ministry, and in affairs pertaining to it. It is also a matter of vast importance how a people receive and treat a faithful minister of Christ, and what use they make of his ministry.

These things have a more immediate and direct bearing on the great and final end for which man was made, and on the eternal welfare of mankind, than any of the temporal concerns of men, whether public or private.

And therefore it is especially fitting that these affairs should be brought into judgment and openly determined and settled in truth and righteousness; and that, to this end, ministers and their people should meet together before the all-knowing and infallible Judge.
2. The mutual concerns of ministers and their people have a special relation to the main things pertaining to the day of judgment.
They have a special relation to that great and divine person who will then appear as Judge.

Ministers are his messengers, sent forth by him; and, in their office and administrations among their people, they represent his person and stand in his place, as those who are sent to declare his mind, to do his work, and to speak and act in his name.
And therefore it is especially fitting that they should return to him to give an account of their work and success.
The king is judge of all his subjects; they are all accountable to him.

But it is more especially necessary that the king’s ministers, who are especially entrusted with the administration of his kingdom, and who are sent out on some special negotiation, should return to him to give an account of themselves, of their discharge of their trust, and of the reception they have met with.

Ministers are not only messengers of the person who on the last day will appear as Judge, but the errand they are sent upon, and the affairs committed to them as his ministers, most immediately concern his honor and the interest of his kingdom.

The work they are sent to do is to promote the designs of his administration and government; and therefore their business with their people has a close relation to the day of judgment; for the great purpose of that day is completely to settle and establish the affairs of his kingdom, to adjust all things that pertain to it, that everything opposed to the interests of his kingdom may be removed, and that everything which contributes to its completeness and glory may be perfected and confirmed, so that this great King may receive his due honor and glory.

Again, the mutual concerns of ministers and their people have a direct relation to the concerns of the day of judgment, as the business of ministers with their people is to promote the eternal salvation of the souls of men and their escape from eternal damnation; and the day of judgment is the day appointed for that end, openly to decide and settle men’s eternal state, to fix some in a state of eternal salvation and to bring their salvation to its utmost completion, and to fix others in a state of everlasting damnation and most perfect misery.
The mutual concerns of ministers and people have a most direct relation to the day of judgment, as the very design of the work of the ministry is the people’s preparation for that day.

Ministers are sent to warn them of the approach of that day, to forewarn them of the dreadful sentence then to be pronounced on the wicked, and to declare to them the blessed sentence then to be pronounced on the righteous, and to use means with them so that they may escape the wrath which is then to come on the ungodly, and obtain the reward then to be bestowed on the saints.

And as the mutual concerns of ministers and their people have so close and direct a relation to that day, it is especially fitting that those concerns should be brought into that day, and there settled and resolved; and that, in order to this, ministers and their people should meet and appear together before the great Judge on that day.

The use I would make of the things which have been observed is to lead the people here present who have been under my pastoral care to some reflections, and to give them some advice suited to our present circumstances, relating to what has lately been done toward our being separated, as to the relation in which we have until now stood to one another; but expecting to meet each other before the great tribunal at the day of judgment.

The deep and serious consideration of that future, most solemn meeting of ours is certainly most suitable at such a time as this, since there has so lately been that done which, in all probability, will (as to the relation we have until now stood in) be followed by an everlasting separation.
How often have we met together in the house of God in this relation!

How often have I spoken to you, instructed, counseled, warned, directed and fed you, and administered ordinances among you, as the people who were committed to my care, and whose precious souls I had charge of!
But in all probability this will never be again.
The prophet Jeremiah (chapter 25,

verse 3) reminds the people how long he had labored among them in the work of the ministry: “From the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, even to this day, that is, the twenty-third year, the word of the Lord came to me, and I have spoken to you, rising early and speaking.”
I am not about to compare myself with the prophet Jeremiah; but in this respect I can say as he did, that “I have spoken the word of God to you into the twenty-third year, rising early and speaking.”
It was twenty-three years, on the 15th day of last February, since I have labored in the work of the ministry in the relation of a pastor to this church and congregation.

And though my strength has been weakness, having always labored under great infirmity of body, besides my insufficiency for so great a charge in other respects, yet I have not spared my feeble strength, but have exerted it for the good of your souls.
I can appeal to you as the apostle does to his hearers, Galatians 4,
verse 13: “You know how through weakness of the flesh I preached the gospel to you.”
I have spent the prime of my life and strength in labors for your eternal welfare.

You are my witnesses that what strength I have had I have not neglected in idleness, nor spent in pursuing worldly schemes and managing temporal affairs for the advancement of my outward estate and the enlarging of myself and my family; but I have given myself wholly to the work of the ministry, laboring in it night and day, rising early and applying myself to this great business to which Christ appointed me.

I have found the work of the ministry among you to be a great work indeed, a work of exceeding care, labor and difficulty: many have been the heavy burdens that I have borne in it, to which my strength has been very unequal.

God called me to bear these burdens; and I bless his name that he has so supported me as to keep me from sinking under them, and that his power in this has been shown in my weakness; so that although I have often been troubled on every side, yet I have not been distressed; perplexed, but not in despair; cast down, but not destroyed.
But now I have reason to think that the work which I had to do as your minister is finished: you have publicly rejected me, and my opportunities cease.
How greatly, therefore, does it now become us to consider that time when we must meet one another before the chief Shepherd!

When I must give an account of my stewardship, of the service I have done for, and the reception and treatment I have had among, the people he sent me to; and you must give an account of your own conduct toward me, and of the use you have made of these twenty-three years of my ministry.

For then both you and I must appear together, and we both must give an account, so that an infallible, righteous and eternal sentence may be passed upon us by him who will judge us with respect to all that we have said or done in our meetings here, all our conduct toward one another, in the house of God and elsewhere, on Sabbath days and on other days; who will try our hearts and reveal our thoughts, and the principles and dispositions of our minds; who will judge us with respect to all the controversies that have existed between us, with the strictest impartiality, and will examine our treatment of each other in those controversies.

There is nothing covered that shall not be revealed, nor hidden that shall not be known; all will be examined in the searching, penetrating light of God’s omniscience and glory, and by him whose eyes are like a flame of fire; and truth and right shall be made to appear plainly, stripped of every veil; and all error, falsehood, unrighteousness and injury shall be laid open, stripped of every disguise; every plausible pretense, every quibble and all false reasoning shall vanish in a moment, as being unable to bear the light of that day.
And then our hearts will be turned inside out, and their secrets will be made to appear more plainly than our outward actions do now.
Then it shall appear what ends we have aimed at, what governing principles we have acted from, and what dispositions we have exercised in our church disputes and contests.

Then it will appear whether I acted uprightly, and from a truly conscientious, careful regard for my duty to my great Lord and Master, in some earlier church controversies, which have been attended with exceedingly unhappy circumstances and consequences; it will appear whether there was any just cause for the resentment that was shown on those occasions.

And then our recent great controversy, concerning the qualifications necessary for admission to the privileges of members in full standing in the visible church of Christ, will be examined and judged in all its parts and circumstances, and the whole will be set forth in a clear, certain and perfect light.

Then it will appear whether the doctrine that I have preached and published concerning this matter is Christ’s own doctrine; whether he will not own it as one of the precious truths that have proceeded from his own mouth, and vindicate and honor it as such before the whole universe.
Then it will appear what is meant by “the man who comes without the wedding garment”; for that is the day spoken of in Matthew 22,
verse 13, in which such a one shall be bound hand and foot and cast into outer darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

And then it will appear whether, in declaring this doctrine, and in acting in agreement with it, and in my general conduct in the affair, I have been influenced by any regard for my own worldly interest or honor, or by a desire to appear wiser than others; or have acted from any sinister, worldly motives whatsoever; and whether what I have done has not been from a careful, strict and tender regard for the will of my Lord and Master, and because I dared not offend him, being satisfied what his will was, after a long, diligent, impartial and prayerful inquiry; having this constantly in view and prospect, to make me greatly concerned not to decide rashly that the truth lies on this side of the question, where I am now persuaded it does: that such a decision would not be for my worldly interest, but every way against it, bringing a long series of extreme difficulties and plunging me into an abyss of trouble and sorrow.

And then it will appear whether my people have done their duty to their pastor with respect to this matter; whether they have shown a right temper and spirit on this occasion; whether they have done me justice in hearing, attending to and considering what I had to say in evidence of what I believed and taught as part of the counsel of God; whether I have been treated with the impartiality, fairness and regard that the just Judge considered due; and whether, in the many steps that have been taken and the many things that have been said and done in the course of this controversy, righteousness and love and Christian decorum have been maintained; or, if otherwise, to how great a degree these things have been violated.

Then every step of the conduct of each of us in this affair, from first to last, and the spirit we have shown in it all, shall be examined and made manifest; and our own consciences shall speak plainly and loudly, and each of us shall be convinced, and the world shall know; and never again shall there be any mistake, misrepresentation or misunderstanding of the affair, to all eternity.

This controversy has now probably been brought to a conclusion between you and me as far as this world is concerned; it was concluded by the event of the week before last. But it must have another decision on that great day, which will certainly come, when you and I shall meet together before the great judgment seat; and therefore I leave it to that time, and shall say no more about it at present.
But I would now proceed to address myself particularly to several kinds of persons.
I. To those among us who profess godliness.
I would now call you to a serious consideration of that great day in which you must meet him who has until now been your pastor, before the Judge whose eyes are like a flame of fire.

I have endeavored, to the best of my ability, to search the word of God with regard to the distinguishing marks of true piety, those by which persons might best discover their state, and most surely and clearly judge themselves.

And I have applied these rules and marks to you from time to time in the preaching of the word, to the utmost of my skill, and in the plainest and most searching manner that I have been able, in order to detect the deceived hypocrite and to establish the hopes and comforts of the sincere.

And yet it is to be feared that, after all I have done, I now leave some of you in a deceived, deluded state; for it is not to be supposed that among several hundred professing Christians, none are deceived.
From now on I am likely to have no more opportunity to take the care and charge of your souls, to examine and search them.

But still I urge you to remember and consider the rules that I have often laid down for you during my ministry, with a solemn regard for the future day when you and I must meet together before our Judge; when the applications calling you to self-examination that you have heard from me must be rehearsed again before you, and those rules of trial must themselves be tried, and it will appear whether they have been good or not; and it will also appear whether you have heard them impartially and tested yourselves by them; and the Judge himself, who is infallible, will try both you and me; and after this no one will be deceived concerning the state of their souls.

I have often reminded you that, whatever your claims to experiences, discoveries, comforts and joys have been, on that day everyone will be judged according to his works; and then you will find it so.

May you have a minister of greater knowledge of the word of God and better acquaintance with the cases of souls, and of greater skill in applying himself to souls, whose sermons may be more searching and convincing; so that those of you who have held fast to deceit under my preaching may have your eyes opened by his; that you may be undeceived before that great day.

What means and helps for instruction and self-examination you may have hereafter is uncertain; but one thing is certain: the time is short, and your opportunity for correcting mistakes in so important a concern will soon come to an end.
We live in a world of great changes.

A great change has now come to pass; you have withdrawn yourselves from my ministry, under which you have continued for so many years. But the time is coming, and will soon come, when you will pass out of time into eternity; and so you will pass from under all means of grace whatsoever.

The greater part of you who profess godliness have (to use the phrase of the apostle) “acknowledged me in part”: you have until now acknowledged me to be your spiritual father, the instrument of the greatest good to you that ever is or can be obtained by any of the children of men.

Consider that day when you and I shall meet before our Judge, when it shall be examined whether you have received from me the treatment that is due to spiritual children, and whether you have treated me as you ought to have treated a spiritual father.

As the relation of a natural parent brings great obligations on children in the sight of God, so much more, in many respects, does the relation of a spiritual father bring great obligations on those whose conversion and eternal salvation they suppose God has made him the instrument of: 1 Corinthians 4,
verse 15: “For though you have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet you have not many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel.”

II. Now that I am taking my leave of this people, I would apply myself to those among them whom I leave in a Christless, graceless condition; and I would call on such to consider seriously that solemn day when they and I must meet before the Judge of the world.

My parting with you is in some respects a peculiarly sorrowful parting, inasmuch as I leave you in most sorrowful circumstances; because I leave you in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity, with the wrath of God abiding on you, and remaining under condemnation to everlasting misery and destruction.
Since I must leave you, it would have been a comforting and happy circumstance of our parting if I had left you in Christ, safe and blessed in that sure refuge and glorious rest of the saints.
But it is otherwise.
I leave you far off, aliens and strangers, wretched subjects and captives of sin and Satan, and prisoners of avenging justice; without Christ and without God in the world.
Your consciences bear me witness that while I had opportunity, I have not ceased to warn you and to set your danger before you.
I have studied to represent the misery and necessity of your circumstances in the clearest manner possible.

I have tried every way I could think of that tended to awaken your consciences, and to make you aware of the necessity of making good use of your time, and of being quick to flee from the wrath to come, and thorough in the use of means for your escape and safety.
I have diligently endeavored to find out and use the most powerful motives to persuade you to take care for your own welfare and salvation.

I have not only endeavored to awaken you, that you might be moved with fear, but I have used my utmost endeavors to win you: I have sought out acceptable words, that if possible I might prevail upon you to forsake sin, and turn to God, and accept Christ as your Savior and Lord.
I have spent my strength very much in these things.
But yet, with regard to you to whom I am now speaking, I have not been successful; but I have reason this day to complain in those words of Jeremiah 6,

verse 29: “The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed by the fire; the refiner melts in vain; for the wicked are not plucked away.” It is to be feared that all my labors, as to many of you, have served no other purpose but to harden you; and that the word I have preached, instead of being a savor of life to life, has been a savor of death to death.

Though I shall not have any account to give in the future for those who have openly and resolutely renounced my ministry, as of a trust committed to me, yet remember that you must give account for yourselves of your care of your own souls, and of your use of all means, past and future, through your whole lives.
God alone knows what will become of your poor, perishing souls, what means you may enjoy hereafter, or what disadvantages and temptations you may be under.

May God in his mercy grant that, however unsuccessful all past means have been, you may have future means that may have a new effect; and that the word of God, as it shall hereafter be dispensed to you, may prove like the fire and the hammer that breaks the rock in pieces.
However, let me now at parting exhort and beseech you not to forget entirely the warnings you have had while under my ministry.

When you and I meet at the day of judgment, then you will remember them: the sight of me, your former minister, on that occasion will soon revive them in your memory, and that in a very affecting manner.
O do not let that be the first time that they are revived in this way.
You and I are now parting from one another as far as this world is concerned; let us labor that we may not be parted after our meeting at the last day.
If I have been your faithful pastor (which will appear on that day, whether I have or not), then I shall be acquitted, and shall ascend with Christ.
O do your part, so that in such a case it may not be that you should be forced to part eternally from me and from all who have been faithful in Christ Jesus.
This is a sorrowful parting that now takes place between you and me, but that would be a more sorrowful parting to you than this.
This one you may perhaps bear without being much affected by it, if you are not glad of it; but such a parting on that day will affect you most deeply, keenly and dreadfully.
III. I would address myself to those who are under some awakenings.

Blessed be God that there are some such, and that (although I have reason to fear I leave multitudes in this large congregation in a Christless state) yet I do not leave them all in total insensibility and carelessness about their souls.

Some of you who I have reason to hope are under some awakenings have made me acquainted with your circumstances; which tends to make me, now that I am leaving you, take my leave of you with a special concern for you.
What will be the outcome of your present exercise of mind I do not know; but it will be known on that day when you and I shall meet before the judgment seat of Christ.
Therefore now give much consideration to that day.

Now that I am parting with this flock, I would once more press upon you the counsels I have given before: to take heed of being superficial in so great a concern, to be thorough and in good earnest in the matter, and to beware of backsliding, to hold on and hold out to the end.
And cry mightily to God that these great changes which are passing over this church and congregation do not prove to be your overthrow.
There is great temptation in them; and the devil will undoubtedly seek to take advantage of them, if possible to make your present convictions and endeavors come to nothing.
You need to double your diligence, and watch and pray, lest you be overcome by temptation.

Whoever may hereafter stand in relation to you as your spiritual guide, my desire and prayer is that the great Shepherd of the sheep would have a special regard for you and be your guide (for there is none who teaches like him), and that he who is the infinite fountain of light would “open your eyes, and turn you from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God; that you may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among those who are sanctified, through faith that is in Christ”; so that on that great day, when I shall meet you again before your Judge and mine, we may meet in joyful and glorious circumstances, never to be separated any more.
IV. I would apply myself to the young people of the congregation.

Since I have been settled in the work of the ministry in this place, I have always had a special concern for the souls of the young people, and a desire that religion might flourish among them; and I have especially exerted myself to that end, because I knew the special opportunity they had beyond others, and that ordinarily those for whom God intended mercy were brought to fear and love him in their youth.

And it has always seemed to me a peculiarly lovely thing to see young people walking in the ways of virtue and Christian piety, having their hearts purified and sweetened with a principle of divine love.

And it has seemed an exceedingly beautiful thing, and one that would greatly adorn the town and add to its happiness, if the young people could be persuaded, when they meet together, to converse as Christians and as the children of God; avoiding impurity, frivolity and excess; keeping strictly to the rules of virtue, and talking together of the things of God and Christ and heaven.
This is what I have longed for; and it has been exceedingly grievous to me when I have heard of vice, vanity and disorder among our youth.

And so far as I know my own heart, it was from this that I formerly led this church to some measures for the suppression of vice among our young people, which gave such great offense, and by which I became so disliked.
I have sought the good, and not the harm, of our young people.

I have desired their truest honor and happiness, and not their disgrace; knowing that true virtue and religion tended not only to the glory and happiness of young people in another world, but to their greatest peace and prosperity, and highest dignity and honor, in this world; and above all things to sweeten and make pleasant and delightful even the days of youth.

But whether I have loved you and sought your good more or less, yet since God in his providence is now calling me to part with you, and I am committing your souls to him who once committed their pastoral care to me, nothing remains but only (as I am now taking my leave of you) earnestly to beseech you, out of love for yourselves if you have none for me, not to despise and forget the warnings and counsels I have so often given you; remembering the day when you and I must meet again before the great Judge of the living and the dead; when it will appear whether the things I have taught you were true, whether the counsels I have given you were good, and whether I truly sought your good, and whether you have made good use of my endeavors.
I have from time to time earnestly warned you against frolicking (as it is called), and against some other liberties commonly taken by young people in the land.

And whatever some may say in justification of such liberties and customs, and however they may laugh at warnings against them, I now leave you my parting testimony against such things, not doubting that God will approve and confirm it on that day when we shall meet before him.
V. I would apply myself to the children of the congregation, the lambs of this flock, who have been so long under my care.
I have just now said that I have had a special concern for the young people; and in saying so I did not intend to exclude you.

You are in youth, and in the earliest youth; and therefore I have been aware that if those who were young had a precious opportunity for their souls’ good, you who are very young had, in many respects, an especially precious opportunity.
And accordingly I have not neglected you: I have endeavored to do the part of a faithful shepherd in feeding the lambs as well as the sheep.

Christ once committed the care of your souls to me as your minister; and you know, dear children, how I have instructed you and warned you from time to time; you know how I have often called you together for that purpose; and some of you have at times seemed to be affected by what I have said to you.

But I am afraid it has had no saving effect on many of you, but that you still remain in an unconverted condition, without any real saving work wrought in your souls, convincing you thoroughly of your sin and misery, causing you to see the great evil of sin, and to mourn for it and hate it above all things, and giving you a sense of the excellence of the Lord Jesus Christ, bringing you with all your hearts to cling to him as your Savior, weaning your hearts from the world, and causing you to love God above all, and to delight in holiness more than in all the pleasant things of this earth; and so I now leave you in a miserable condition, having no interest in Christ, and so under the awful displeasure and anger of God, and in danger of going down to the pit of eternal misery.
But now I must bid you farewell: I must leave you in the hands of God; I can do no more for you than pray for you.
Only I ask you not to forget, but often to think of the counsels and warnings I have given you, and the endeavors I have made, that your souls might be saved from everlasting destruction.
Dear children, I leave you in an evil world that is full of snares and temptations.
God alone knows what will become of you.
This the Scripture has told us, that there are but few saved; and we have abundant confirmation of it from what we see.
This we see: that children die as well as others; multitudes die before they grow up; and of those who grow up, comparatively few ever give good evidence of saving conversion to God.

I pray God to pity you, and take care of you, and provide for you the best means for the good of your souls; and that God himself would undertake for you, to be your heavenly Father and the mighty Redeemer of your immortal souls.
Do not neglect to pray for yourselves: take heed that you are not among the number of those who cast off fear and restrain prayer before God.
Pray to God constantly in secret; and often remember that great day when you must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, and meet your minister there, who has so often counseled and warned you.
I conclude with a few words of advice to all in general, on some particulars that are of great importance for the welfare and prosperity of this church and congregation.
1. One thing that greatly concerns you, if you would be a happy people, is the maintaining of family order.

We have had great disputes about how the church ought to be regulated; and indeed the subject of these disputes was of great importance; but the proper regulation of your families is of no less, and in some respects of much greater, importance.
Every Christian family ought to be, as it were, a little church, consecrated to Christ, and wholly influenced and governed by his rules.
And family education and order are some of the chief means of grace.
If these fail, all other means are likely to prove ineffectual.
If these are duly maintained, all the means of grace will be likely to prosper and be successful.

Let me now, therefore, once more, before I finally cease to speak to this congregation, repeat and earnestly press the counsel I have often urged on heads of families here while I was their pastor: to take great pains in teaching, warning and directing their children; bringing them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord; beginning early, where there is still opportunity, and maintaining a constant diligence in labors of this kind; remembering that, if you would not have all your instructions and counsels prove ineffectual, there must be government as well as instruction, which must be maintained with an even hand and steady resolution, as a guard to the religion and morals of the family and the support of its good order.

Take heed that it is not with any of you as it was with Eli of old, who rebuked his children but did not restrain them; and that by this means you do not bring a similar curse on your families as he did on his.
And let children obey their parents, and yield to their instructions, and submit to their orders, if they would inherit a blessing and not a curse.

For we have reason to think, from many things in the word of God, that nothing tends more to bring a curse on persons in this world, and on all their worldly concerns, than undutiful, unsubmissive, disorderly behavior in children toward their parents.
2. If you would seek the future prosperity of this society, it is of vast importance that you avoid contention.
A contentious people will be a miserable people.

The contentions that have been among you since I first became your pastor have been one of the greatest burdens I have labored under in the course of my ministry: not only the contentions you have had with me, but those you have had with one another about your lands and other concerns; because I knew that contention, heat of spirit, evil speaking and things of a similar nature were directly contrary to the spirit of Christianity, and in a peculiar manner tended to drive God’s Spirit away from a people and to render all means of grace ineffectual, as well as to destroy a people’s outward comfort and welfare.
Let me therefore earnestly exhort you, as you would seek your own future good, to watch against a contentious spirit.
If you would see good days, seek peace and pursue it, 1 Peter 3,
verses 10, 11. Let the contention that has lately arisen about the terms of Christian communion, as it has been the greatest of your contentions, also be the last of them.
I would, now that I am preaching my farewell sermon, say to you, as the apostle said to the Corinthians, 2 Corinthians 13,
verses 11, 12: “Finally, brothers, farewell.
Be perfect, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you.”
And here I would particularly advise those who have stood by me in the recent controversy to watch over their spirits and avoid all bitterness toward others.
Your temptations are in some respects the greatest, because what has recently been done is grievous to you.

But however wrongly you may think others have acted, maintain with great diligence and watchfulness a Christian meekness and calmness of spirit; and labor in this respect to excel others who are of the opposing side.
And this will be the best victory: for “he who rules his spirit is better than he who takes a city.”
Therefore let nothing be done through strife or vainglory.

Indulge no revengeful spirit in any way, but watch and pray against it; and by all means in your power seek the prosperity of the town; and never think that you behave as becomes Christians except when you sincerely, feelingly and fervently love all men, of whatever party or opinion, and whether friendly or unkind, just or injurious, to you or your friends, or to the cause and kingdom of Christ.
3. Another thing that vastly concerns the future prosperity of this town is that you should watch against the encroachments of error, and particularly Arminianism and doctrines of a similar tendency.
Many of you, as I well remember, were much alarmed at the apprehension of the danger of these corrupt principles prevailing, nearly sixteen years ago.
But the danger then was small in comparison with what appears now.

These doctrines are at this day much more prevalent than they were then: the progress they have made in the land within these seven years seems to have been vastly greater than at any time in a similar span before; and they are still prevailing and creeping into almost all parts of the land, threatening the utter ruin of the credit of those doctrines that are the peculiar glory of the gospel, and of the interests of vital piety.
And I have lately perceived some things among yourselves that show that you are far from being out of danger, but on the contrary are remarkably exposed.

The older people may perhaps think themselves sufficiently fortified against infection; but it is fitting that all should beware of self-confidence and carnal security, and should remember those needful warnings of sacred Scripture, “Do not be high-minded, but fear,” and “let him who stands take heed lest he fall.”
But let the case of the older people be as it may, the rising generation is doubtless greatly exposed.
These principles are exceedingly appealing to corrupt nature, and are what young people, at least those who do not have their hearts established with grace, are easily led away by.

And if these principles should greatly prevail in this town, as they very recently have done in another large town I could name, formerly greatly noted for religion, and so for a long time, it will threaten the spiritual and eternal ruin of this people in the present and future generations.
Therefore you need the greatest and most diligent care and watchfulness with respect to this matter.
4. Another thing I would advise, that you may hereafter be a prosperous people, is that you give yourselves much to prayer.
God is the fountain of all blessing and prosperity, and he will be sought for his blessing.
I would therefore advise you not only to be constant in secret and family prayer, and in the public worship of God in his house, but also often to assemble yourselves in private prayer societies.

I would advise all who are grieved for the afflictions of Joseph, and deeply affected by the calamities of this town, whatever their opinion regarding the subject of our recent controversy, to meet together often for prayer, and to cry to God for his mercy to themselves, and mercy to this town, and mercy to Zion and the people of God in general throughout the world.

5. The last article of advice I would give (which doubtless greatly concerns your prosperity) is that you take great care with regard to the settling of a minister, to see who, or what kind of person, he is whom you settle; and particularly in these two respects:
(1) That he be a man of thoroughly sound principles in the scheme of doctrine that he maintains.
This you will stand in the greatest need of, especially in such a day of corruption as this.
And in order to obtain such a one, you will need to exercise extraordinary care and prudence.
I know the danger.

I know the manner of many young gentlemen of corrupt principles, their ways of concealing themselves, the fair, plausible disguises they are accustomed to put on, by which they deceive others, in order to maintain their own credit, and get themselves into others’ confidence and employment, and secure and establish their own interest, until they see a convenient opportunity to begin more openly to broach and spread their corrupt tenets.
(2) Labor to obtain a man who has an established character as a person of serious religion and fervent piety.
It is of vast importance that those who are settled in this work should be men of true piety, at all times and in all places; but more especially at some times, and in some towns and churches.
And this present time, which is a time in which religion is in danger from so many corruptions in doctrine and practice, is in a peculiar manner a day in which such ministers are necessary.

Nothing but sincere piety of heart is at all to be depended on, at such a time as this, as a security to a young man just coming into the world against the prevailing infection, or to engage him thoroughly in proper and successful endeavors to withstand and oppose the torrent of error and prejudice against the high, mysterious, evangelical doctrines of the religion of Jesus Christ, and their genuine effects in true experiential religion.
And this place is one that especially needs such a minister, for reasons obvious to all.

If you should happen to settle a minister who knows nothing truly of Christ and the way of salvation by him, nothing experientially of the nature of vital religion, alas, how exposed you will be, like sheep without a shepherd!
Here in this place there is need of one who shall be eminently fit to stand in the gap and make up the hedge, and who shall be like the chariots of Israel and its horsemen.
You need one who shall stand as a champion in the cause of truth and the power of godliness.
Having briefly mentioned these important articles of advice, nothing remains but that I now take my leave of you and bid you all farewell, wishing and praying for your best prosperity.
I would now commend your immortal souls to him who formerly committed them to me, expecting the day when I must meet you again before him who is the Judge of the living and the dead.
I desire that I may never forget this people, who have been so long my special charge, and that I may never cease to pray fervently for your prosperity.

May God bless you with a faithful pastor, one who is well acquainted with his mind and will, thoroughly warning sinners, wisely and skillfully searching professing Christians, and leading you in the way to eternal blessedness.
May you truly have a burning and shining light set up in this candlestick; and may you, not only for a season but during his whole life, and that a long life, be willing to rejoice in his light.

And let me be remembered in the prayers of all God’s people who are of a calm spirit, and are peaceable and faithful in Israel, of whatever opinion they may be with respect to the terms of church communion.
And let us all remember, and never forget, our future solemn meeting on that great day of the Lord; the day of infallible decision and of the everlasting and unalterable sentence. Amen.
